newsitem.title: USA: Thai yankee debut to withstand Moody's downgrade.
newsitem.headline: Thai yankee debut to withstand Moody's downgrade.

text.p: Demand for the Kingdom of Thailand's first Yankee bond issue is expected to be strong enough to override concerns about a credit downgrade in a cautious U.S. interest rate environment, U.S. analysts and traders said.
"It shows Thailand's confidence to proceed with the issue," on the heel of the downgrade, said Feroz Talyarkhan, director of Asian fixed income at Bear, Stearns & Co Inc.
The bond will most likely be issued in two tranches for a total of $500 million, a source familiar with the issue said.
Since the Yankee borrowing plan was made public in March, the Thai financial market has been rocked by failures of financial institutions and repeated rumors of a currency devaluation.
Pressure on the country's creditworthiness culminated when Moody's Investors Service late Tuesday downgraded the country's long-term foreign currency debt to A3 from A2.
Mitigating the negative implications of Moody's downgrade was steadfast support from rival agency, Standard and Poor's.
In two teleconferences last week, S&P strongly defended the existing single-A rating, which it, as expected, assigned to Thailand's $500 million Yankee bond issues on Wednesday.
Unlike Moody's focus on Thailand's current disarray in financial markets, S&P zeroed in on Thailand's potential to weather the storm, Talyakhan said.

Nancy Northrop, vice president at Alliance Capital, said lead manager Lehman Brothers and high-ranking Thai officials, also made highly commendable efforts to allay investors' fears about the country's banking woes.
A roadshow to promote the Yankee issues was taking place in New York on Wednesday.
Traders said a cautious mood in the bond market had more impact on the Yankee's launch than pure sovereign concerns.
"Rising long bond yields made people more interested in the 10-year tranche," a trader said.
Price talk centered around 85 to 90 basis points (bps) over U.S. Treasuries, which had widened from 75 to 80 bps when the deal was first announced, according to market sources.
The 30-year tranche was expected to fetch 110 bps over Treasuries, they said.
Another trader noted that buyers were still enthusiastic about the sovereign credit, although they were cooling on Thai corporate issues.
"I have no doubt the kingdom's Yankee will sell," said another trader. "It's a museum piece -- rare and well-bid."
The steady tone in the Thai stock market, even on the banks that were directly affected by Moody's downgrade, also sent a positive signal to foreign investors, said Talyarkhan at Bear, Stearns.
But some inertia might be due to the reluctance to take positions before the long weekend holiday in Thailand, he added. "We would know better when the market opens next week."
Monday the market is closed for the Songkran Festival Day.
